claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are governed by atomic-scale defects and electronic structure.
Vacancies, dislocations, and grain boundaries are the relevant atomic-scale structural mediators.
Atomic-scale defects and electronic structure influence deformation mechanisms including dislocation glide and twinning.
Changes in dislocation glide and twinning affect alloy hardness and strength.
The relevant behavior can be investigated using first-principles calculations or molecular-dynamics simulations.
Under room-temperature, quasi-static loading, the high-entropy alloys will exhibit a 10–20% increase in hardness and strength relative to the conventional-alloy baseline.
The average conventional-alloy baseline is approximately 500 MPa strength and 200 HV hardness.
The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys containing 5–10 elements.
The hypothesis applies over a grain-size range of 1–10 micrometres.
The magnitude of strengthening may depend on alloy composition and processing conditions.
A controlled comparison should vary the levels of atomic-scale defects and electronic structure while measuring hardness, strength, grain size, and defect density.
The hypothesis is falsified if hardness and strength fail to increase by at least 5% relative to the baseline.
